statement: Whether Nzambi a Mpungu originally denoted a benevolent creator/sky-father (the older ethnographic-synthesis reading, reflected in most popular sources) is disputed by Wyatt MacGaffey's most recent textual work. MacGaffey, "Precolonial Beliefs in God, Nzambi, and Chthonic Beings: Evidence from Kongo Texts," Journal of Religion in Africa 52(1-2), 2022, using early-20th-century manuscripts by indigenous ethnographers drawing on Karl Laman's ~10,000-page manuscript collection (Protestant converts, c. 1915), argues Nzambi's original semantic field centered on death, with the life/creation valence instead carried by bisimbi (chthonic, land/water-associated spirit forces). The "benevolent creator" framing reflects the post-missionary Christianized gloss on Nzambi once the term was repurposed to translate the Christian God.
scholarly_disagreement: Whether Nzambi a Mpungu's original precolonial meaning centered on death (MacGaffey 2022) or was already a benevolent creator/sky-father (older ethnographic synthesis).

sources.citation: MacGaffey, Wyatt. "Precolonial Beliefs in God, Nzambi, and Chthonic Beings: Evidence from Kongo Texts." Journal of Religion in Africa 52(1-2), 2022: 1-21.
sources.author: Wyatt MacGaffey

interpretations.position: Nzambi a Mpungu was originally a personification of death; bisimbi carried the life/creation valence
interpretations.strongest_case: Direct textual analysis of the early-20th-century Laman manuscript collection, written by indigenous ethnographers close in time to living precolonial memory.

interpretations.position: Nzambi a Mpungu was already a high-god/creator sky-father figure in the precolonial period

holders.name: Older ethnographic synthesis tradition, e.g. K.K. Bunseki Fu-Kiau

interpretations.strongest_case: This is the dominant framing across most 20th-century ethnography and remains the majority popular/reference-work position.
